solution_options.fusion_note: Low-level data fusion of synchronised Raman and MIR-ATR spectra taken from the same sampling spot, with each block scaled and calibrated separately. The fused model must beat the best single method on held-out runs before the extra instrument is kept.

citations.quote: It is crucial that the spectral information obtained by different methods-Mid-IR, NIR, Raman, and fluorescence spectra-is collected from the same small, even pinpoint, area of the sample.
Ultimately, the measurement data must be normalized to a common time step.
If the variables have different units of measurement, the data should be normalized in some way, for example, using an autoscaling algorithm.

chemometrics_note: Quantitative glucose and lactate need calibration models (for example PLS) built on reference laboratory values. These models are matrix-specific and should be validated on held-out runs, then re-checked when the medium or cell population changes.
realtime_tracking_note: The point of the pilot is in-line, continuous tracking. If more than one method is used, the data from each method must be aligned to a common time step before fusion.
future_direction: If the pilot succeeds, a compact optical multisensor system or a spectral fiber sensor for routine control could be considered later.

proposal.what_would_change_it: A high fluorescence background or strongly changing turbidity could shift the choice toward MIR-ATR or a combined probe. If one method cannot meet the required accuracy, the extended option becomes relevant.
proposal.next_step: Run a multi-method laboratory trial on representative medium samples, with the existing laboratory glucose and lactate values as reference.

brief_answer: Test Raman first: it suits aqueous media and has been used to detect glucose and lactate directly in a reactor. MIR-ATR is a complementary single method to compare, and NIR transmission only if the medium stays clear. Combining Raman and MIR-ATR is a later hypothesis. The pilot can be checked against your existing laboratory measurements. Concentration ranges, medium turbidity and required accuracy are still open.
